name: Multi-interest modeling and generative retrieval
venue_year: MIND CIKM 2019; ComiRec KDD 2020; SUM 2021; P5 RecSys 2022; TIGER NeurIPS 2023; LETTER CIKM 2024; OneRec 2025
release_and_license: ComiRec's public repository was live but displayed no repository license through the GitHub API; P5's public repository was live under MIT. MIND, SUM, TIGER, LETTER and OneRec have primary papers, but a complete author-maintained code/data release with unambiguous reusable terms was not verified for every work [uncertain]. Paper availability does not grant permission to reuse industrial datasets.
input_history: MIND, ComiRec and SUM encode a sequence of previously interacted items into multiple latent interest vectors or channels. TIGER and LETTER convert catalog items into semantic-code sequences and condition an autoregressive model on earlier item codes. P5 converts histories, item metadata and tasks into natural-language templates. OneRec encodes historical video behavior and generates a session-sized recommendation sequence.
prediction_target: The original targets are mostly the next interacted item, a withheld item, or a generated recommendation session. MIND/ComiRec retrieve candidate items; SUM predicts sequential behavior; TIGER/LETTER generate the next item's identifier; P5 includes sequential recommendation among several text-to-text tasks; OneRec generates videos and optimizes aggregate/session preference. None of these primary task definitions explicitly targets the set of future semantic interests absent from the user's frozen history.
novel_interest_definition: The audited works generally do not define novel interest. Multiple interest vectors mean multiple aspects already inferred from H(u), diversity means a varied recommendation list, cold item means limited item-side interaction history, and a new semantic-ID sequence means a newly generated item identifier. None is equivalent to Y_new(u)=F(u)-H(u) at a declared semantic granularity.
novelty_granularity_and_reference_window: Original evaluations usually score item IDs relative to the preceding interaction sequence. They do not stratify whether the target is a new item in a known category, a new leaf category, a new ancestor category, or merely semantically distant. For CrossInterest, attach a frozen taxonomy to every event and compute novelty against the entire declared H window, not only the last item or active-interest vector.
interest_onset_definition: Original models usually treat the held-out interaction as the label, regardless of whether it repeats a known interest. CrossInterest should define onset independently of the architecture: first future purchase/strong engagement in a previously absent semantic category, followed by an optional persistence window. A model-generated interest phrase or semantic code is a prediction, not onset evidence.

is_direct_match.MIND, ComiRec, SUM: Transferable method-only matches for representing several historical interests; their evaluations do not isolate history-absent future interests.
is_direct_match.TIGER and LETTER: Transferable method-only matches for semantic item tokenization, constrained generation and cold-item generalization; semantic IDs are latent item identifiers, not novel-interest labels.
is_direct_match.P5: Transferable prompting/text-generation framework; its unified tasks do not by themselves create a valid new-interest target.
is_direct_match.OneRec: Transferable session-wise generation and preference-alignment method; online watch-time lift is not an isolated new-interest result.
is_direct_match.query and hierarchical category generati: A promising CrossInterest adaptation, but not directly validated by these works: generate explicit taxonomy paths or retrieval queries and score only history-absent future concepts.

persistence_signal: The representative papers evaluate one held-out next item, a recommendation list/session, or overall online engagement. They generally do not require the newly predicted semantic interest to recur later. OneRec's session-wise generation captures within-request coherence, not longitudinal adoption. CrossInterest must reserve a later window and label one-off versus repeated new-category engagement.

method.multi-interest extraction: MIND uses capsule dynamic routing over behaviors plus label-aware attention; ComiRec uses multi-interest extraction and a controllable accuracy-diversity aggregation; SUM maintains multiple incremental interest channels with erase-add updates and attention.
method.semantic-ID retrieval: TIGER learns residual-quantized semantic IDs from item content, then autoregressively predicts the next item's code sequence. LETTER jointly regularizes tokenization with hierarchical semantics, collaborative alignment and code diversity, and adds ranking-guided generation.
method.language generation: P5 casts user/item/review tasks as personalized text-to-text prompts. A CrossInterest variant could generate a human-readable query or taxonomy path, then retrieve items under that concept.
method.unified/session generation: OneRec replaces retrieve-then-rank with encoder-decoder session generation, sparse MoE capacity and iterative reward-model/DPO preference alignment.
method.recommended composition: Use a multi-interest encoder for H, an explicit exploration head for concepts absent from H, constrained hierarchical decoding, and a separate item retriever. Do not force the exploration head to reconstruct only observed-interest vectors.

evaluation_protocol: The audited literature mainly uses chronological leave-one-out/next-item evaluation with Recall/Hit Rate/NDCG and sometimes list diversity, cold-item buckets or online aggregate engagement. This does not answer the CrossInterest question because repeat targets dominate and negatives may be sampled. Re-evaluate every method on a frozen H/F split with explicit Y_new, full-catalog or contemporaneous-candidate ranking, separate repeat/explore strata, category-level exactness, user-level bootstrap intervals and a later persistence window.
generalization_axis: MIND/ComiRec/SUM emphasize user-interest capacity and next-item retrieval; TIGER reports improved retrieval for items with no prior interaction history, which is item cold-start rather than user-new interest; LETTER improves item tokenization/ranking; P5 emphasizes cross-task zero/few-shot transfer; OneRec emphasizes industrial scale and preference alignment. Add seen-user future-new-category and held-out-user future-new-category axes explicitly.
exposure_handling: The representative offline benchmarks generally use logged positives and sampled or catalog negatives without randomized exposure or impression propensities. Their models therefore learn from MNAR interactions. OneRec's reward model simulates preference pairs because only one list is displayed, but this is not randomized exposure identification. CrossInterest should use exposed/randomized subsets where available and report unlabeled-catalog evaluation separately.
main_findings_and_limits: The methods provide strong building blocks but no direct evidence that they predict future interests absent from history. Multi-interest encoders can improve recall by covering established tastes; diversity controls can add variety without accuracy on true new interests; semantic IDs help item retrieval and cold items but can encode popularity/collaboration; LLM prompting can verbalize plausible interests without behavioral grounding. The key research contribution should therefore be the target construction and repeat-versus-explore evaluation, not merely swapping in a larger generator.
scale: MIND includes public benchmarks plus a large industrial Tmall deployment; ComiRec evaluates Amazon and Taobao; SUM uses two sequential datasets; P5 uses several established recommendation tasks; TIGER/LETTER use multiple public recommendation datasets; OneRec reports Kuaishou deployment. Exact processed-user/item/event counts depend on each paper's filtering and should be recovered from frozen preprocessing artifacts before reproduction [uncertain].
stable_user_identity: All sequential evaluations assume a stable user or session history within their processed datasets, but papers often split each user's sequence rather than test identity durability across long real-world windows. OneRec's session generation and some industrial logs may emphasize request/session continuity. Dataset-level stable identity must be audited independently; a session or playlist key cannot substitute for a user key.
timestamps_and_order: Models consume ordered interaction sequences, but ordering is not always equivalent to precise event time and paper preprocessing often keeps only relative order. CrossInterest requires original timestamps, deterministic tie handling and frozen history/future cutoffs; order-only public derivatives cannot support calendar horizons, seasonality or opportunity controls [uncertain].
left_censoring_and_history_coverage: Multi-interest models treat observed history as sufficient input but do not establish that it covers the user's prior lifetime interests. Short or truncated sequences can make an old interest appear novel. Semantic-ID and LLM models do not solve this measurement problem. Apply minimum-history and burn-in gates, vary H length, and describe targets as newly observed within the dataset.
item_semantics: MIND/ComiRec/SUM can run on ID/category embeddings and do not require human-readable semantics. TIGER creates content-based residual-quantized codes; LETTER adds hierarchical semantic, collaborative and diversity regularization. P5 uses textual metadata and reviews. OneRec generates video identifiers in an industrial system. CrossInterest should retain human-readable taxonomy labels alongside latent codes so predictions and novelty checks remain auditable.
feedback_and_exposure: The methods are usually trained on positive interactions such as clicks, purchases, ratings or watches; explicit impressions, positions and propensities depend on the underlying dataset and are generally absent from public evaluations. OneRec aligns to a learned reward and reports watch time; that outcome remains policy-dependent. Use feedback strength to define onset before model training rather than letting each model redefine the label.
candidate_space: MIND/ComiRec retrieve by nearest interests from an item pool; TIGER/LETTER decode semantic IDs under a catalog trie or identifier vocabulary; P5 may generate item tokens/text; OneRec generates a session directly. These mechanisms can cover large catalogs, but the papers do not reconstruct historical availability or actual exposures. For category generation, constrain decoding to the frozen taxonomy and then retrieve only contemporaneously eligible items.
taxonomy_and_opportunity_drift: Latent semantic-ID hierarchies are learned codebooks and need not align with human category ancestors. A prefix shared by two IDs is therefore not automatically an interpretable interest. Re-training tokenizers across time can also change code meanings. Freeze tokenizer/taxonomy versions, store item first-seen times and inventory eligibility, and prevent future text, popularity or collaborative signals from entering the tokenizer [uncertain].
construct_h_f_ynew: Use the same leakage-safe dataset builder for every architecture: H(u) is the frozen sequence before cutoff; F(u) is strong future behavior; Y_new(u) contains future taxonomy concepts absent from all of H. Feed only H to MIND/ComiRec/SUM, TIGER/LETTER, P5 or OneRec adaptations. Add two heads: repeat-item/category retrieval and exploration-category generation. For the exploration head, mask concepts already present in H during constrained decoding, then retrieve items under generated concepts. Score against Y_new before scoring item ranking.
leakage_and_missingness_risks: Risks include target-aware interest selection during training, future category/text features in semantic tokenizers, collaborative codebooks trained on dev/test interactions, popularity leakage, random rather than temporal splits, sampled-negative inflation, session/user conflation, post-cutoff taxonomy drift, LLM memorization and plausible-but-ungrounded generated queries. Fit tokenizers, concept vocabularies, popularity and retrieval indices on training-time data only and preserve hashes.

recommended_role.MIND/ComiRec/SUM: Primary encoder baselines and ablations for whether multiple historical-interest slots improve new-category forecasting.
recommended_role.TIGER/LETTER: Primary generative-retrieval baselines for semantic item codes and constrained catalog decoding.
recommended_role.P5: Natural-language query/category generation baseline, with strict grounding and closed-vocabulary evaluation.
recommended_role.OneRec: Method inspiration for multi-item/session decoding and preference alignment; reproduction is limited by industrial data/code availability.
recommended_role.new CrossInterest model: Hybrid: explicit repeat/explore separation, interpretable taxonomy-path generation, candidate retrieval and persistence-aware training.

priority: High: re-evaluate ComiRec or MIND and TIGER or LETTER under the identical Y_new protocol. Medium: P5-style text query generation and SUM's incremental interests. Method inspiration only: OneRec until reproducible artifacts exist. The first gate is a strong popularity/category-transition baseline; do not scale an LLM before proving user-conditioned signal.
verification_status: Primary-source abstracts/papers verified the task formulations and architectural claims for MIND, ComiRec, SUM, P5, TIGER, LETTER and OneRec. Live repositories and licenses were checked for ComiRec and P5. Exact per-dataset preprocessing counts, negative construction and complete code/license status for every work remain [uncertain]. No audited primary evaluation was found that explicitly filters targets to semantic interests absent from the full user history.
repeat_explore_and_persistence_audit: Re-run every baseline with four disjoint labels: repeat item, new item within known concept, first observed concept and sustained first observed concept. Report the fraction of test positives in each group before metrics. Measure whether each latent interest slot maps to known-history concepts or contributes to Y_new. A diverse list containing unseen categories counts only if future behavior confirms the category, and persistence requires another later positive after onset.
evidence_quotes_or_schema_facts: MIND explicitly represents a user with multiple vectors and learns them by clustering historical behaviors; the paper frames evaluation as matching/recommendation, not history-absent interest forecasting.
ComiRec's abstract formalizes the task as predicting the next items and controls the balance between recommendation accuracy and diversity.
SUM maintains multiple interest channels with erase-and-add updates for large-scale sequential recommendation.
TIGER trains a sequence-to-sequence model to predict the Semantic ID of the next item and separately reports better retrieval for items with no prior interaction history.
LETTER integrates hierarchical semantics, collaborative signals and code-assignment diversity into a learnable tokenizer; its target remains generative recommendation/ranking.
P5 converts interactions, descriptions, metadata and reviews into text-to-text tasks and supports personalized prompts, zero-shot and few-shot transfer.
OneRec generates a session of videos and uses a reward model plus iterative DPO; its reported 1.6% watch-time lift is an aggregate online result, not a new-interest stratum.
